questions.prompt: In his reading of Job, what makes a tragedy more than 'bad things happen'?
choices: A Comedy mixed with slapstick.
B Terrible things happening in an unjust way—especially worst things to the least deserving.
C Any inconvenience at an airport.
D Losing a game you deserved to lose.
questions.explain: Tragedy is unjust suffering; the ultimate tragedy is the worst happening to the least deserving.

questions.prompt: What does the book Ordinary Men illustrate about ordinary people and evil?
choices: A Only lifelong sadists commit atrocities.
B Step by step, ordinary middle-aged policemen can become perpetrators of horrific acts.
C Propaganda never influences behavior.
D Leaving when ordered to stay is impossible for humans.
questions.explain: Ordinary Men shows ordinary policemen going along, step by step, until they become worst murderers—relevant to you.

questions.prompt: What Solzhenitsyn line does he cite about truth and totalitarianism?
choices: A Lying more efficiently strengthens the state.
B One man who stops lying can bring down a totalitarian state.
C Truth is irrelevant under any government.
D Only armies, never individuals, matter.
questions.explain: He quotes Solzhenitsyn: one man who stops lying can bring down a totalitarian state—minor foolishnesses aren't trivial.

questions.prompt: In Cain and Abel, what contrast does he draw about sacrifice?
choices: A Abel refuses all sacrifice; Cain invents capitalism.
B Abel represents proper sacrifice; Cain makes second-rate sacrifices (for reasons you must examine in yourself).
C Both brothers make identical offerings.
D Sacrifice is only about livestock prices.
questions.explain: Abel = proper sacrifice pattern; Cain = second-rate sacrifices—and you have your own reasons for cutting corners.

questions.prompt: What stance does Job take that Peterson presents as courageous rather than naive?
choices: A Immediate nihilistic rejection of being.
B Refusing to lose faith in existence/God despite unjust misery—and assuming goodwill rather than bitter resentment.
C Celebrating injustice as a game.
D Pretending suffering never happened.
questions.explain: Job refuses the nihilistic conclusion despite unjust misery; the fitting attitude is courageous faith, not naive denial.
